questions.stem: A satellite image of the Earth's night-time lights shows the largest bright clusters in eastern North America, Europe, South Asia and East Asia. These clusters mainly show the global pattern of:
options: agricultural production, especially irrigated grain and rice crops
areas with the highest rainfall and the most fertile volcanic soils
areas where international tourism makes up most of the economy
settlement and infrastructure such as cities, roads and power grids
questions.explanation: Night-time lights come from electrified settlements, transport routes and industry, so they map where people live and where infrastructure is concentrated. Farmland is mostly dark at night, which is why productive farming regions do not stand out.

questions.stem: Wet rice farming is concentrated in the river valleys and deltas of monsoon Asia. Which combination of factors best explains this spatial pattern of agricultural production?
options: dense rainforest cover, poor drainage and few people
summer monsoon rain, flat floodplains and plentiful labour
cool winters, deep frosts and thin glacial soils on steep slopes
low rainfall, steep terrain and highly mechanised farms
questions.explanation: Paddy rice needs large amounts of water, level land that can be flooded and, traditionally, a lot of labour, all of which monsoon floodplains and deltas provide. Steep, dry or frost-prone land is unsuited to flooded paddies.

questions.stem: Since the late 20th century, much of the world's manufacturing output has shifted from Europe and North America to East Asia. Which set of factors best explains this global shift?
options: the exhaustion of coal in Europe and the end of global trade agreements
a decline in demand for manufactured goods in all wealthy countries
lower labour costs, investment by TNCs and cheaper container shipping
rising tariffs in Asia, falling populations and rising energy costs
questions.explanation: Transnational corporations moved production to places with lower costs, and containerisation made it cheap to ship goods back to distant markets. Demand in wealthy countries did not fall; it was increasingly met by imports.

questions.stem: Spanish and Portuguese are the dominant languages across most of Central and South America. This spatial pattern of culture is best explained by:
options: the spread of Spanish-language television and music through satellites
trade agreements that require member countries to share a language
colonisation and settlement from the Iberian Peninsula from the 1500s
recent migration of workers from Spain and Portugal since the 1990s
questions.explanation: Spain and Portugal colonised most of the region from the 16th century, and their languages, religion and institutions became dominant. Modern media reinforce the pattern but did not create it.

questions.stem: In geography, 'time-space compression' refers to:
options: the crowding of more people into the same area as cities grow denser
the shortening of growing seasons in places affected by climate change
the way faster transport and communication make distant places feel closer
the shrinking of continents as tectonic plates converge over geological time
questions.explanation: Time-space compression describes how technologies such as jet aircraft, containerisation and the internet reduce the time and cost of moving people, goods and information. The absolute distance between places does not change.

questions.stem: A flight from Sydney to London took several days in the 1950s but now takes about a day. Geographically, this shows that between the two cities:
options: relative distance has risen because the number of flights has grown
relative distance has fallen while absolute distance is unchanged
absolute distance has fallen while relative distance is unchanged
both absolute and relative distance have fallen by the same amount
questions.explanation: Absolute distance is the fixed physical distance in kilometres. Relative distance is measured in time, cost or effort, and that is what faster aircraft have reduced.

questions.stem: A smartphone is designed in the United States, uses components made in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and is assembled in China before being sold worldwide. This best shows the role of TNCs in:
options: organising global production networks that integrate distant places
keeping each stage of production within a single national economy
reducing trade between countries by producing goods where they are sold
spreading production evenly so all countries gain equal value from it
questions.explanation: TNCs split production into stages located wherever costs and skills suit them, linking places in a global production network. The value is not shared equally: design and branding usually capture much more of it than assembly.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a world city such as London or New York?
options: a command centre of the global economy, with headquarters, finance and global links
any city with a population above ten million, whatever its role in the world economy
a capital city that hosts the national government and the national parliament
a city whose economy is based mainly on manufacturing goods for export markets
questions.explanation: World (global) cities are defined by their function: they concentrate corporate headquarters, finance, law and media and are highly connected to other cities. Some very large cities have far less global influence, so population alone does not make a world city.

questions.stem: According to the International Organization for Migration, about how many people were living outside their country of birth in 2020?
options: about 28 million, or around 0.4% of the world's population
about 1.2 billion, or around 15% of the world's population
about 2.8 billion, or around 36% of the world's population
about 281 million, around 3.6% of the world's population
questions.explanation: The IOM estimated about 281 million international migrants in 2020, roughly 3.6% of all people. Although migration is a major force for integration, most people still live in the country where they were born.

questions.stem: When international borders closed in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, several small island countries suffered sharp falls in income. What does this most clearly show about tourism and integration?
options: tourism reduces integration, because visitors stay only a short time
dependence on international tourism exposes places to global shocks
tourism links are weaker than trade links, so they rarely matter
island economies are self-sufficient once tourism stops completely
questions.explanation: Tourism ties local jobs and incomes to the movement of people from distant places, so a global disruption hits tourism-dependent economies directly. Their economic losses show that tourism links mattered a great deal.

questions.stem: A student argues that because the internet allows instant communication, all places are now equally connected. Which is the strongest response?
options: Places were equally connected before the internet, so nothing has changed at all
The internet connects places only within countries, never between countries
Access is uneven, so time-space compression has drawn some places closer than others
The internet has made places less connected, because people now travel less often
questions.explanation: Connectivity depends on infrastructure, cost and skills, so a digital divide remains between and within countries. Technological change has compressed time and space most for already well-connected places.

questions.stem: UN estimates for 2024 put Niger's total fertility rate at about 6 children per woman. Japan's total fertility rate in the same estimates was closest to:
questions.explanation: Japan's total fertility rate was about 1.2 in 2024, well below the replacement level of about 2.1. Niger's was about five times higher, one of the highest in the world.

questions.stem: UN estimates put the median age in Niger at about 15 years in 2024, compared with about 49 years in Japan. A median age of about 15 means that:
options: the average person in Niger dies at about 15 years of age
most people in Niger have children by the age of 15
people in Niger are counted as adults from the age of 15
half of Niger's population is younger than about 15
questions.explanation: The median age divides a population into two equal halves, one younger and one older. A very low median age is the result of high fertility, which keeps adding large numbers of children; it says nothing directly about life expectancy.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains Niger's very high fertility?
options: late marriage, high housing costs and very long working hours for parents
strict government limits on family size and widespread contraceptive use
high urbanisation and a large share of women in professional jobs
early marriage, low female schooling and children valued for farm labour
questions.explanation: Niger has one of the highest rates of child marriage in the world, few girls complete secondary school and most families depend on rain-fed farming, where children contribute labour and old-age support. High child mortality also encourages large families.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains Japan's very low fertility?
options: high infant mortality that discourages couples from having children
late marriage, few births outside marriage and the high cost of raising children
early marriage, low female schooling and a mainly rural farming economy
a government policy that limits each couple to a single child by law
questions.explanation: In Japan most births occur within marriage, so the trend to later marriage and more people never marrying sharply reduces births. Long working hours, housing costs and education costs also discourage larger families. Japan has never had a legal limit on family size.

questions.stem: The status of women helps explain the very different fertility of Japan and Niger. Which statement best explains how?
options: Japanese women's long schooling and careers delay births; early marriage in Niger lengthens childbearing
Women in both countries marry at the same age, so status cannot explain the gap in fertility
Niger's women have more years of schooling than Japan's, which raises the demand for children
Japan's women marry younger than Niger's, but government policy prevents them having children
questions.explanation: Long education and paid work, with limited support for combining them with family, delay marriage and births in Japan. In Niger, early marriage and little schooling mean women start childbearing young and have many more years in which to have children.

questions.stem: In 2024, about 47% of Niger's people were aged under 15 and about 3% were 65 or over. In Japan, about 11% were under 15 and about 29% were 65 or over. Which comparison of dependency is correct?
options: Both countries have the same dependency ratio, since only the age mix differs
Niger has almost no dependants, because so few of its people are elderly
Niger's overall dependency ratio is higher, made up mostly of children
Japan's overall dependency ratio is higher, because the elderly outnumber children
questions.explanation: Niger's dependants make up about 50% of the population (about 97 per 100 working-age people), while Japan's make up about 40% (about 68 per 100). Japan's dependants are mainly elderly, but its total burden is lower than Niger's mainly youthful one.

questions.stem: Niger's population is growing by more than 3% a year, and most people depend on rain-fed farming in the Sahel. Which challenge does this growth most directly intensify?
options: a shrinking workforce, as too few young people enter the local labour market
a surplus of empty housing, as rural villages lose most of their people
rising pension costs, as the share of people over 65 grows rapidly
food insecurity, as farms are subdivided and spread onto drought-prone land
questions.explanation: Rapid growth adds pressure to a limited area of farmland in a drought-prone environment, raising the risk of food shortages and land degradation. A shrinking workforce and rising pension costs are challenges of ageing countries such as Japan.

questions.stem: Niger's 'schools for husbands', set up with UNFPA support from 2007, respond to high fertility and maternal deaths by:
options: legally limiting each couple to three children, with fines for extra births
sending women overseas for education so that they marry at a later age
training respected married men to promote health centres and family planning
paying couples a cash bonus for each year that they do not have another child
questions.explanation: The schools bring together husbands who meet regularly with health workers and then encourage other men to support antenatal care, supervised births and family planning. They target men because husbands often decide whether wives use health services.

questions.stem: In 2023 Japan set up a Children and Families Agency and expanded child allowances and childcare. This approach to population management is best described as:
options: antinatalist
restrictive
eugenic
pronatalist
questions.explanation: Pronatalist policies aim to raise the birth rate, here by reducing the costs and difficulties of raising children. Antinatalist policies aim to reduce births, the opposite of Japan's goal.

questions.stem: Since the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development in Cairo, the internationally agreed approach to population management has emphasised:
options: national birth quotas enforced through fines rather than voluntary programs
reducing migration rather than changing levels of fertility or mortality
raising birth rates in all countries rather than lowering them anywhere
reproductive rights and individual choice rather than demographic targets
questions.explanation: The Cairo conference shifted the focus from meeting population targets to meeting people's needs, including education for girls, health care and access to family planning by choice. Coercive targets and quotas were rejected.

questions.stem: In debates about Niger's population, some religious and community leaders value large families as a blessing, while health officials promote spacing births. What best explains why these perspectives differ?
options: They rely on different census figures, since Niger's population is unknown
Health officials want to raise fertility, while community leaders want to lower it
Both groups agree on large families, so there is no real difference
They rest on different values, such as religious belief versus health risks
questions.explanation: Varying perspectives on population management usually come from different values and priorities, such as religious and cultural beliefs about family versus concern for maternal and child health. Both groups accept that fertility is high; they disagree about whether that is a problem.

questions.stem: A country's ecological footprint is:
options: the number of people the country's farmland could feed at current yields
the quantity of non-renewable resources still remaining within its borders
the area of productive land and water needed to supply its resources and absorb its wastes
the total land area of the country, including its deserts, mountains and ice
questions.explanation: The ecological footprint, measured in global hectares, compares human demand on nature with biocapacity, the area available to meet it. It is a measure of consumption, not of a country's size or reserves.

questions.stem: The Global Footprint Network estimates that humanity uses resources about 1.7 times as fast as the Earth's ecosystems can regenerate them. This means that:
options: only 1.7% of the Earth's natural resources are still available for human use
the world's population is 1.7 times what it was a generation ago
the Earth could support 1.7 times as many people as it does today
people are running down natural capital, such as fish stocks and forests
questions.explanation: Using more than the planet regenerates each year (ecological overshoot) is possible only by depleting stocks and accumulating wastes such as carbon dioxide. It describes the rate of consumption, not the size of the population.

questions.stem: Using the relationship I = P × A × T (impact = population × affluence × technology), a country's population rises by 10% while consumption per person falls by 10%, with technology unchanged. Its environmental impact:
options: falls by about 1%
stays exactly the same
rises by about 1%
falls by about 10%
questions.explanation: The new impact is 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99 of the original, a fall of about 1%. The changes multiply rather than add, so a 10% rise and a 10% fall do not cancel exactly.

questions.stem: Most of the world's mined cobalt, used in batteries for phones and electric cars, comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while most batteries are used elsewhere. This best illustrates that natural resources are:
options: unevenly distributed and often consumed far from where they are extracted
evenly distributed, so every country can meet its own needs from local supplies
consumed mainly in the places where they are mined and processed
renewable, because new deposits form as quickly as they are mined
questions.explanation: Resource deposits are concentrated by geology, while consumption is concentrated in wealthy and industrial places. Global trade links the two, so the environmental costs of extraction and the benefits of use often fall on different people.

questions.stem: Canada closed the northern cod fishery off Newfoundland in 1992 after stocks collapsed from decades of heavy fishing. This is an example of:
options: environmental degradation caused mainly by natural climate cycles
depletion of a renewable resource harvested faster than it could recover
depletion of a non-renewable resource that cannot ever be replaced by nature
a resource shortage caused mainly by a fall in demand for the fish
questions.explanation: Fish stocks are renewable only if harvesting stays below their rate of reproduction. Overfishing ran the stock down so far that the fishery was closed, costing thousands of jobs.

questions.stem: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) sets out the principle of free, prior and informed consent. Applied to a proposed mine on Indigenous lands, this means:
options: the company may proceed if it pays compensation after the mine opens
the national government alone decides once it has held a public meeting
consent is needed only if the mine will be visible from a settlement
the community must be informed and agree before the project goes ahead
questions.explanation: Free, prior and informed consent requires full information, no pressure and agreement before a project starts. Resource extraction without it has often cost Indigenous Peoples access to land, water, food sources and cultural sites.

questions.stem: Rainforest in Indonesia and Malaysia has been cleared for oil palm plantations to supply products sold around the world. This best shows how resource consumption can cause:
options: degradation that is caused entirely by local population growth
environmental degradation in places far from where products are consumed
environmental improvement, because plantations store more carbon than forest
resource depletion only in the countries where the products are bought
questions.explanation: Demand from distant consumers drives land clearing, habitat loss and carbon emissions in producing regions. The degradation is linked to global consumption, not only to the size of the local population.

questions.stem: Some countries with large oil or mineral exports have low levels of human wellbeing. Which explanation best accounts for this inequality?
options: Countries with resources have no need for health care or education
Wellbeing depends only on population size, not on income or resources
Resource wealth is captured by elites, and other parts of the economy are neglected
Resource exports always lower national income, so wellbeing must fall
questions.explanation: The 'resource curse' describes how revenue from resources can be concentrated in few hands, encourage corruption and crowd out farming and manufacturing. Resource exports raise national income, but that income is often shared very unequally.
